guide.title: Magnetic fields and electromagnetism: review guide
guide.intro: Moving charges create magnetic fields and feel magnetic forces. This unit covers both sides, using the Biot–Savart law for any current and Ampère's law for symmetric ones.

sections.title: Magnetic forces on charges and currents
body: A charge moving through a magnetic field feels F = qv × B, with magnitude |q|vB sin θ, perpendicular to both v and B. The force does no work, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed. Moving perpendicular to a uniform field, a charge circles with radius r = mv/(|q|B) and period T = 2πm/(|q|B), which does not depend on its speed.
A current-carrying wire feels F = IL × B; for a curved wire, integrate dF = I dl × B. In a uniform field, any wire's net force equals the force on a straight wire joining its ends.
points: With crossed electric and magnetic fields, a charge passes straight through when v = E/B (a velocity selector).
Reverse the right-hand-rule direction for negative charges.
A closed current loop in a uniform field feels no net force, though it can feel a torque.

sections.title: Fields of long current-carrying wires
body: A long straight wire's field circles it with magnitude B = μ₀I/(2πr): point your right thumb along the current, and your fingers curl the way B goes.
Two parallel wires push or pull on each other with force per length F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd): currents in the same direction attract, and opposite currents repel.
points: The field falls off as 1/r, not 1/r².
Fields from several wires add as vectors.
A wire's own field exerts no net force on itself.

sections.title: The Biot–Savart law and Ampère's law
body: The Biot–Savart law gives the field of a small piece of current: dB = (μ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r². Integrating it gives, for example, B = μ₀I/(2R) at the center of a circular loop.
Ampère's law, ∮B·dl = μ₀I_enc, gives B quickly when the current has symmetry: inside a long solenoid B = μ₀nI, and inside a long solid wire with uniform current B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²).
points: Choose an Amperian loop along which B is constant and parallel to the path.
Outside an ideal long solenoid, B ≈ 0.
In this course, Ampère's law is applied to steady currents.

example.prompt: A long solenoid has 1200 turns along 0.60 m and carries 2.5 A. Find the magnetic field inside it.
example.solution: n = 1200/0.60 = 2000 turns per meter, so B = μ₀nI = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(2000)(2.5) ≈ 6.3 × 10⁻³ T, directed along the axis.

misconceptions: “Magnetic forces can speed a charge up.”
They act perpendicular to the velocity, so they do no work.
“A long wire's field falls off as 1/r².”
Currents in the same direction attract.
“Ampère's law holds only for symmetric currents.”
It always holds; symmetry is what makes it easy to solve for B.

questions.prompt: An electron moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.20 T magnetic field. What is the size of the magnetic force on it? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
choiceExplanations: The force is zero only for motion along the field; this electron moves perpendicular to it.
6.0 × 10⁵ is vB; the electron's charge is left out.
3.2 × 10⁻²⁰ is qB; the speed is left out.

questions.prompt: A proton circles in a uniform magnetic field. Its speed is then doubled (still perpendicular to the field). What happens to the radius and the period of its circle?
choices: The radius doubles and the period stays the same
The radius halves and the period doubles
questions.explanation: r = mv/(|q|B) is proportional to v, so it doubles. T = 2πm/(|q|B) doesn't depend on v: the faster proton travels a bigger circle in the same time.
choiceExplanations: The period doesn't depend on speed; the longer path is covered at a higher speed.
A faster particle needs a larger radius, not a smaller one.
The radius depends on speed, so it changes.

questions.prompt: A wire bent into a semicircle of radius 0.10 m carries 5.0 A and lies in a plane perpendicular to a uniform 0.20 T magnetic field. What is the net magnetic force on the semicircle?
questions.explanation: In a uniform field, the net force on any wire equals the force on a straight wire joining its ends. The ends are a diameter, 2R = 0.20 m, apart: F = I(2R)B = (5.0)(0.20)(0.20) = 0.20 N.
choiceExplanations: 0.31 N uses the arc length πR; the forces on different parts of the arc point in different directions and partly cancel.
The forces don't cancel completely; only a closed loop gives zero net force in a uniform field.
0.10 N uses the radius instead of the distance between the ends.

questions.prompt: A long straight wire carries 20 A. What is the magnetic field 0.10 m from it? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
choiceExplanations: 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ T divides by r²; a long wire's field falls off as 1/r.
2.5 × 10⁻⁴ T leaves out the 2π in the denominator.
The field circles the wire; it isn't zero at points beside it.

questions.prompt: Two long parallel wires, 0.050 m apart, each carry 10 A in the same direction. What is the force per meter between them? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = (2 × 10⁻⁷)(10)(10)/0.050 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ N/m. Currents in the same direction attract.
choiceExplanations: Currents in the same direction attract; opposite currents repel.
2.0 × 10⁻⁵ leaves out the division by d.
8.0 × 10⁻³ divides by d² instead of d.

questions.prompt: A long solenoid has 2000 turns per meter and carries 1.5 A. What is the magnetic field inside it? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: From Ampère's law, B = μ₀nI = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(2000)(1.5) ≈ 3.8 × 10⁻³ T.
choiceExplanations: 1.9 × 10⁻³ T halves the correct value; there is no factor ½ in B = μ₀nI.
6.0 × 10⁻⁴ T divides by 2π as if it were a straight wire.
3000 is nI; it must be multiplied by μ₀.

questions.prompt: A long, solid cylindrical wire of radius R carries current I spread uniformly over its cross-section. What is the magnetic field at a distance R/2 from its axis?
questions.explanation: An Amperian circle of radius r = R/2 encloses I(r/R)² = I/4. Then B(2πr) = μ₀I/4, so B = μ₀(I/4)/(2π · R/2) = μ₀I/(4πR). In general, B = μ₀Ir/(2πR²) inside.
choiceExplanations: μ₀I/(πR) treats all of I as enclosed by the circle; only a quarter of it is.
μ₀I/(2πR) is the field at the wire's surface, r = R.
The field is zero only on the axis; at r = R/2 some current is enclosed.

questions.prompt: A circular loop of radius 0.10 m carries 2.0 A. What is the magnetic field at its center? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A)
questions.explanation: From the Biot–Savart law, every piece of the loop is a distance R from the center and perpendicular to the line to it, so B = (μ₀I/4πR²)(2πR) = μ₀I/(2R) = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(2.0)/(0.20) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ T.
choiceExplanations: 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ T uses μ₀I/(2πR), the long straight wire's formula.
6.3 × 10⁻⁶ T is μ₀I/(4R), the field of a half loop.
2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T leaves out the 2 in μ₀I/(2R).

questions.prompt: In a velocity selector, an electric field of 2000 V/m and a perpendicular magnetic field of 0.010 T act on moving charges. At what speed does a charge pass straight through?
questions.explanation: It passes straight through when the forces balance: qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2000/0.010 = 2.0 × 10⁵ m/s, whatever its charge or mass.
choiceExplanations: 20 multiplies E and B; the speed is their ratio.
5.0 × 10⁻⁶ is B/E, the ratio upside down.
2000 is the electric field strength alone.
